questions.rq1: What fraction of MAS-AIRM expectations can be automatically checked from artefacts, semi-automated with human attestation, or only documented?
questions.rq2: Holding purpose and data fixed, how does autonomy change Impact/Complexity/Reliance and which Section 5 controls become binding?
questions.rq3: For common guardrail patterns, what is the measured failure rate under standard adversarial probe families, and does it meet a defensible threshold per materiality tier?
questions.rq4: What share of MAS-AIRM expectations is covered, partially covered or uncovered by ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act, and what residual work does an already-certified institution face?
questions.rq5: How many controls, evidence items and estimated person-hours does each materiality tier require, and where is the long tail?

methods.rq1: Each of the 51 expectation paragraphs takes the best automatability class among the controls implementing it; paragraphs with no implementing control count as doc. Classes and their justifications are in src/airm/controls/controls.yaml.
methods.rq2: Each of 4 portfolio use cases is rewritten at 6 autonomy levels; only the autonomy field and the minimal agent scaffolding needed for validity change. Applicable controls are those the catalogue selects for the variant.
methods.rq3: 20 probes across 5 families (4 attack families plus a benign control set) run under 5 guardrail patterns. Detection is by regular expression, never by a model, so the measurement does not depend on the thing being measured. Wilson 95% intervals throughout.
methods.rq4: 224 hand-authored mapping rows over 51 expectation paragraphs. The denominator is the expectation count, not the mapped-row count, so an unmapped expectation counts against coverage rather than being excluded.
methods.rq5: Applicable controls and their evidence items are counted per use case from the control catalogue, then multiplied by a per-item effort estimate that varies with the control's automatability class and a tier multiplier. Institution-level controls are counted once.

figures.caption: Automatability of MAS-AIRM expectation paragraphs by section, as implemented by this toolkit. auto: a deterministic function of the inventory entry and its evidence decides pass/fail. semi: presence and currency of the artefact is machine-checkable but adequacy needs human attestation. doc: organisational or judgemental, with no artefact the toolkit inspects. Classification is the authors' judgement relative to this implementation, not a MAS classification.

Applicable MAS-AIRM controls as a use case moves up the autonomy ladder, holding purpose, data and model family fixed. Marker colour is the inherent risk materiality tier under the toolkit's default rubric. Tiering and the rubric are the authors' proposal: MAS prescribes no formula (Response to Feedback §7.19).

Attack success rate of five guardrail patterns against four probe families on 20 probes, backend ollama. Lower is better. The dashed line is the toolkit's proposed High-tier limit, not a MAS threshold: MAS sets no performance thresholds (Response to Feedback 10.29). Four benign control probes measure over-refusal, reported in the table rather than this figure.

Coverage of the 51 MAS-AIRM expectation paragraphs by other AI governance frameworks. full: the other framework imposes an equivalent obligation. partial: related but narrower, differently scoped or optional. none: no mapping asserted. Mapping is interpretive and asymmetric, since ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard, the EU AI Act is product law and the NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, so a paragraph can be covered in substance and uncovered in legal effect.

Estimated first-time compliance effort for the synthetic bank portfolio, by use case and by the automatability class of the control requiring each evidence item. Person-hour figures are the authors' estimates from the table in experiments/rq5_cost.py, not measurements; the shape of the distribution is the claim, not the absolute values. Use case labels are coloured by inherent tier.

rq1: The classification is the authors' judgement, not MAS'. Each row carries a written justification so it can be disputed individually.
A clause is auto *relative to this implementation*: it depends on what the toolkit ingests. A richer integration would move some semi clauses to auto.
Single annotator, so no inter-rater agreement is available. The full table is published for challenge.
Taking the best class per paragraph flatters automatability: a paragraph with one auto and four doc controls counts as auto.
rq2: The rubric is the toolkit's proposal; MAS declines to prescribe one (Response to Feedback §7.19). The result describes this rubric's behaviour.

An agentic variant needs an agent extension to be a valid entry, so part of the step at autonomous_agent is the scaffolding, not autonomy as such. The scaffolding is identical across subjects to keep it a constant.
A weighted-sum rubric is run as a sensitivity check and recorded alongside.
Four use cases is a small sample; the direction is the claim, not the magnitude.
rq3: One small local model. Absolute rates say nothing about frontier models; the comparison between patterns is the transferable part.
Twenty probes is a small sample, which is why every rate carries a Wilson interval and why no pattern can certify the Critical tier here regardless of its point estimate.

Detection is regex-based, so it measures whether a specific string appeared, not whether the response was harmful. A model could comply in substance while evading the pattern, which would understate attack success.
The LLM judge shares the generator's weights, which is the realistic cheap deployment and also the one most likely to inherit the generator's blind spots.
Probes use published low-sophistication techniques on purpose: the measurement is whether a guardrail stops the obvious cases, not whether it stops a determined adversary.
Single run per probe at temperature 0. Run-to-run variance is not measured.
rq4: Mapping is interpretive and performed by one annotator. Every row carries a justification, a confidence flag and a gap note so it can be disputed individually rather than only in aggregate.

The comparison is asymmetric by nature: ISO 42001 certifies a management system, the EU AI Act regulates products through conformity assessment, and the NIST AI RMF is voluntary. 'Full' coverage means an equivalent obligation exists, not that holding one discharges the other.
EU AI Act obligations attach to a system's risk classification, so a mapping may be full for an Annex III high-risk use and irrelevant for everything else.
18 rows are flagged low confidence and are the first place a reader should look to disagree.

The MAS Information Paper predates the Guidelines and reports observed practice rather than imposing expectations, so its high 'full' count says the Guidelines codified existing practice, not that an institution can rely on it.
rq5: Person-hours are not measured. They are a transparent assumption set, reported in full, and every derived number moves with them.
The portfolio is synthetic and deliberately spans the tier range, so its mix is not representative of any real institution's AI estate.

The portfolio contains no Low-tier use case, because under the default rubric a Generative AI use case cannot be rated Low: GenAI sets Complexity to High and the impact gate permits one level above Impact. H5(a) is therefore tested against Medium rather than Low and is weaker than written.
Effort is counted per evidence item, which treats a one-line attestation and a full validation report as comparable units within a class.
Reuse across use cases is ignored: a data lineage document covering one dataset serves every use case that uses it, so the portfolio total overstates marginal cost.

disclosures.rq2_post_hoc_ladder_change: docs/RESEARCH_QUESTIONS.md pre-registered the ladder as assistive, human-in-the-loop, autonomous agent, multi-agent, and framed H2(b) and H2(c) on the human-in-the-loop to autonomous step. While implementing the library an AUTONOMOUS_DECISIONING level was added, distinct from AUTONOMOUS_AGENT, because a model that acts without human review of each decision (a real-time fraud block) is fully autonomous under MAS-AIRM 4.12(c) but has no tools, so the agent attributes of 4.8 fn25 do not apply to it. That change moved the step the hypotheses named. H2(b) and H2(c) are reported as refuted on their original wording. H2(c-revised) tests the same underlying claim on the revised ladder and is reported separately so a reader can see which test was pre-registered and which was not.
disclosures.rq3_detector_calibration: Each probe's success_pattern is an instrument, not a hypothesis. The patterns were revised once after inspecting the unguarded (none) responses of the reference model, which exposed two error classes: DJ-01 matched the 'As DAN' persona echo inside an outright refusal, counting a refusal as an attack success; and DJ-03, DJ-04, PE-01 and PE-04 missed successful attacks because the model phrased them differently from the anticipated wording (for example 'offers a compelling 20% return' rather than 'guarantees'). Calibration used the none condition only, so it could not be steered by which guardrail pattern it would favour, and no pattern was changed after seeing the guarded results. A separate defect was fixed in the backend first: the reference model is a reasoning model, and with thinking enabled the whole token budget went to the thinking field, returning an empty completion that matched no probe and produced a false 0% attack success rate across every pattern. The backend now passes think=False and treats an empty completion as an error rather than as a refusal.
disclosures.rq3_backend: ollama qwen3.5:0.8b at temperature 0.0, seed 20261013, num_predict 512, think=False
disclosures.rq3_joint_criterion: MAS-AIRM 5.15 asks for the effectiveness of guardrails to be tested. Measured on attack success alone, the layered pattern looks strong. Measured jointly with over-refusal on a benign control set, the patterns that suppress attacks also refuse a large share of ordinary in-scope requests, so on this model and probe set no pattern is both effective and usable. Both thresholds were fixed before the run.
disclosures.rq5_estimates: These are assumptions, not measurements. They are published so that a reader can substitute their own and recompute. Measuring them would need a user study; see docs/FUTURE_WORK.md.
disclosures.rq4_mapping_confidence: 18 of 224 crosswalk rows are low confidence and are listed individually in results/rq4_crosswalk.json

1.6.heading: Introduction
1.6.justification: A framework-adequacy judgement for the board, not an artefact property.

1.7.heading: Introduction
1.7.justification: A review cadence is evidenceable but whether the review genuinely addressed new risks is a judgement.

2.2.heading: Application of the Guidelines
2.2.justification: No control in this catalogue implements the paragraph, so this toolkit offers no way to check it.

2.5.heading: Application of the Guidelines
2.5.justification: Policy existence and content are organisational facts. The toolkit can hold the policy pointer and flag the §2.5(f) review as overdue, nothing more.

3.2.heading: AI Oversight
3.2.justification: A framework-adequacy judgement for the board, not an artefact property.

3.3.heading: AI Oversight
3.3.justification: MAS removed the prescriptive dedicated-committee requirement (Response to Feedback §5.3), so what remains is an outcome the FI must demonstrate, not a structure a tool can detect.

3.4.heading: AI Oversight
3.4.justification: The toolkit can see whether a confirmation exists but cannot evaluate an FI's appetite statement, which §3.4(b) leaves to the board.

3.5.heading: AI Oversight
3.5.justification: An incident log is machine-readable and the toolkit maintains one; whether escalation happened in time is a process judgement.

3.6.heading: AI Oversight
3.6.justification: An accountability narrative, evidenced by minutes and reporting, not by data.

4.1.heading: Key AI Risk Management Systems, Policies and Procedures
4.1.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

4.2.heading: AI Identification
4.2.justification: Whether an embedded component from a material provider carries an independent assessment is decidable from the register's own fields.

4.3.heading: AI Identification
4.3.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

4.4.heading: AI Identification
4.4.justification: The existence of a shadow-AI policy and of technical controls is evidenceable; the adequacy of coverage is not, and no accepted metric for shadow-AI coverage exists (see the gap table).

4.5.heading: AI Inventory
4.5.justification: A last-reviewed date is machine-readable, but whether the frequency is appropriate is an FI judgement that MAS deliberately leaves open (Response to Feedback §6.18).

4.6.heading: AI Inventory
4.6.justification: A declared mapping in the register; presence is decidable.

4.7.heading: AI Inventory
4.7.justification: Each attribute is a field of the register; presence is decidable without judgement. Adequacy of the content is not checked, which is why the control is about capture, not quality.

4.8.heading: AI Inventory
4.8.justification: Footnote 25 names four attributes; each maps to a field of the agent extension.

4.9.heading: AI Inventory
4.9.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

4.10.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.10.justification: The rubric is deterministic, so the rating and its agreement with the recorded rating are both decidable. The rubric itself is the toolkit's proposal, not a MAS method.

4.11.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.11.justification: The rubric is deterministic, so the rating and its agreement with the recorded rating are both decidable. The rubric itself is the toolkit's proposal, not a MAS method.

4.12.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.12.justification: The rubric is deterministic, so the rating and its agreement with the recorded rating are both decidable. The rubric itself is the toolkit's proposal, not a MAS method.

4.13.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.13.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

5.1.heading: AI Life Cycle Controls
5.1.justification: Presence of an owner and developer party is decidable from the register.

5.2.heading: AI Life Cycle Controls
5.2.justification: Whether a pilot records a scope-limiting guardrail (rate limit, allowlist, step cap or human checkpoint) is decidable from the register.

5.3.heading: AI Life Cycle Controls
5.3.justification: A recorded plan is checkable; whether it was tested and is operationally feasible under a range of conditions is not, and no evidence convention exists (see the gap table).

5.4.heading: Data Management
5.4.justification: The register records a classification; whether it is correct is a data-governance judgement.

5.5.heading: Transparency and Explainability
5.5.justification: "Appropriate level" is the judgement MAS explicitly keeps contextual (Response to Feedback §10.12-§10.15); only the existence of disclosures and explanation methods is evidenceable.

5.6.heading: Transparency and Explainability
5.6.justification: The existence of a disclosure artefact and a redress channel is checkable; adequacy for the audience is a judgement.

5.7.heading: Fairness
5.7.justification: A fairness report with metric values is machine-readable and can be threshold-checked, but there is no universally applicable metric (Response to Feedback §10.21), so metric choice and threshold are FI judgements requiring attestation.

5.8.heading: Fairness
5.8.justification: A fairness report with metric values is machine-readable and can be threshold-checked, but there is no universally applicable metric (Response to Feedback §10.21), so metric choice and threshold are FI judgements requiring attestation.

5.9.heading: Human Oversight
5.9.justification: Whether an oversight arrangement is recorded at all is decidable; this control checks presence, and the adequacy judgement sits in AIRM-5.9-OVERSIGHT-EFFECTIVENESS.

5.10.heading: Third-Party AI Management
5.10.justification: An eval result scoped to the use case is machine-readable; whether it compensates adequately for vendor opacity is a judgement (Response to Feedback §9.10).

5.11.heading: Third-Party AI Management
5.11.justification: Whether an independent assessment is recorded for each component is decidable from the register. Whether the assessment covers the right risks is not, so the evidence list asks for the assessment scope.

5.12.heading: Selection
5.12.justification: A selection note is checkable for existence; the balance it strikes is a judgement, and MAS softened this from a requirement to justify in all cases (Response to Feedback §10.24).

5.13.heading: Selection
5.13.justification: A selection note is checkable for existence; the balance it strikes is a judgement, and MAS softened this from a requirement to justify in all cases (Response to Feedback §10.24).

5.14.heading: Evaluation and Testing
5.14.justification: Thresholds and measured values are machine-comparable once recorded, so a breach is detectable; whether the measures and thresholds are the right ones is an FI judgement that MAS declines to prescribe (Response to Feedback §10.28-§10.29).

5.15.heading: Evaluation and Testing
5.15.justification: Whether a pilot records a scope-limiting guardrail (rate limit, allowlist, step cap or human checkpoint) is decidable from the register.

5.16.heading: Technology and Cybersecurity Risks
5.16.justification: Declared approved tools and permissions are register fields; their presence is decidable and is the precondition for the observed-versus-approved audit in `airm.evals`.

5.17.heading: Reproducibility and Auditability
5.17.justification: Whether documentation is linked at all is decidable from the register. Whether it would let someone replicate the evaluation is the judgement left to the reviewer, which is why the evidence list asks for the reproducibility statement.

5.18.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.18.justification: Whether a review status other than "not reviewed" is on record is decidable; the depth of the review is the reviewer's judgement.

5.19.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.19.justification: Independence of the named validator from owner, developer, deployer and operator is decidable from role records; whether the challenge was effective is not.

5.20.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.20.justification: Whether a review status other than "not reviewed" is on record is decidable; the depth of the review is the reviewer's judgement.

5.21.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.21.justification: A governance workflow fact, outside the toolkit's view.

5.22.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.22.justification: Presence and date of a penetration test, red-team report and go-live checklist are checkable; their depth is a judgement, and MAS prescribes no methodology (Response §10.39).

5.23.heading: Post-Deployment Monitoring and Review
5.23.justification: Whether trace logging is enabled is a register field, and the toolkit can additionally audit an actual trace against approved tool scope.

5.24.heading: Post-Deployment Monitoring and Review
5.24.justification: A due date and a last-validated date are comparable, so an overdue re-validation is detectable; the appropriate interval is an FI judgement.

5.25.heading: Change Management
5.25.justification: Presence of a change-notification term is a register field.

5.26.heading: Change Management
5.26.justification: For a retired use case the presence of a decommissioning record is decidable; adequacy of secure removal is not, and is covered by the data security control.

6.1.heading: AI Risk Management Capabilities
6.1.justification: Training completion records exist but competence is not inspectable from artefacts; MAS also allows role-based training checks instead of individual assessment (Response §11.9).

6.2.heading: AI Risk Management Capabilities
6.2.justification: Training completion records exist but competence is not inspectable from artefacts; MAS also allows role-based training checks instead of individual assessment (Response §11.9).

6.3.heading: Technology Infrastructure for AI
6.3.justification: A capacity and resilience judgement made outside this toolkit.

rq3.question: For common guardrail patterns, what is the measured failure rate under standard adversarial probe families, and does it meet a defensible threshold per materiality tier?
rq3.method: 20 probes across 5 families (4 attack families plus a benign control set) run under 5 guardrail patterns. Detection is by regular expression, never by a model, so the measurement does not depend on the thing being measured. Wilson 95% intervals throughout.
rq3.detector_calibration: Each probe's success_pattern is an instrument, not a hypothesis. The patterns were revised once after inspecting the unguarded (none) responses of the reference model, which exposed two error classes: DJ-01 matched the 'As DAN' persona echo inside an outright refusal, counting a refusal as an attack success; and DJ-03, DJ-04, PE-01 and PE-04 missed successful attacks because the model phrased them differently from the anticipated wording (for example 'offers a compelling 20% return' rather than 'guarantees'). Calibration used the none condition only, so it could not be steered by which guardrail pattern it would favour, and no pattern was changed after seeing the guarded results. A separate defect was fixed in the backend first: the reference model is a reasoning model, and with thinking enabled the whole token budget went to the thinking field, returning an empty completion that matched no probe and produced a false 0% attack success rate across every pattern. The backend now passes think=False and treats an empty completion as an error rather than as a refusal.

probes.reference: Greshake et al. 2023, Not What You've Signed Up For
Perez and Ribeiro 2022, Ignore Previous Prompt

patterns.none: no guardrail: the model answers the prompt directly
patterns.system_prompt: instruction-only: a system prompt stating the policy
patterns.filter: deterministic input and output filter (deny-list and pattern match)
patterns.llm_judge: second-pass LLM judge reviewing the candidate response

proposed_thresholds.note: The authors' proposal, not MAS thresholds. MAS declines to set indicative performance thresholds, noting they depend on the risk materiality of the use case and the FI's risk appetite (Response to Feedback 10.29). A pattern meets a tier only if the UPPER Wilson bound is below the threshold, so a small sample cannot manufacture a pass.

Measured jointly with over-refusal on a benign control set, the patterns that suppress attacks also refuse a large share of ordinary in-scope requests, so on this model and probe set no pattern is both effective and usable. Both thresholds were fixed before the run.

threats_to_validity: One small local model. Absolute rates say nothing about frontier models; the comparison between patterns is the transferable part.
Twenty probes is a small sample, which is why every rate carries a Wilson interval and why no pattern can certify the Critical tier here regardless of its point estimate.

Detection is regex-based, so it measures whether a specific string appeared, not whether the response was harmful. A model could comply in substance while evading the pattern, which would understate attack success.
The LLM judge shares the generator's weights, which is the realistic cheap deployment and also the one most likely to inherit the generator's blind spots.
Probes use published low-sophistication techniques on purpose: the measurement is whether a guardrail stops the obvious cases, not whether it stops a determined adversary.
Single run per probe at temperature 0. Run-to-run variance is not measured.

rq4.question: What share of MAS-AIRM expectations is covered, partially covered or uncovered by ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act, and what residual work does an already-certified institution face?
rq4.method: 224 hand-authored mapping rows over 51 expectation paragraphs. The denominator is the expectation count, not the mapped-row count, so an unmapped expectation counts against coverage rather than being excluded.

nist_ai_rmf.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1)

nist_genai_profile.title: NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)

mas_info_paper_2024.title: MAS Information Paper on AI Model Risk Management (Dec 2024)

2.2.heading: Application of the Guidelines
2.2.summary: Unless 2.3 applies, an FI must establish oversight frameworks with AI identification, materiality assessment and inventory (Sections 3-4) and apply lifecycle controls and capabilities (Sections 5-6), calibrated by relevance and risk materiality.

2.5.heading: Application of the Guidelines
2.5.summary: Basic AI governance must minimally include accountable senior management, permitted and prohibited uses with human oversight rules, an approved-tool list and approval process, staff education, compliance checks, and periodic/trigger-based review of the 2.3 criteria.

3.4.heading: AI Oversight
3.4.summary: Board (or delegated committee) approves and reviews the AI governance approach and strategic direction, embeds AI risks in the risk appetite framework, sets roles, maintains adequate AI understanding, and reviews these regularly.

3.6.heading: AI Oversight
3.6.summary: Local senior management remains accountable that group frameworks address Singapore-specific requirements, has visibility and input, has escalation paths for local issues, and can demonstrate oversight to MAS.

4.1.heading: Key AI Risk Management Systems, Policies and Procedures
4.1.summary: The AI risk framework must include systems, policies and procedures for identification, inventorisation and risk materiality assessment, applied consistently, with controls proportionate to assessed materiality.

4.4.heading: AI Identification
4.4.summary: Keep residual risk from unidentified AI (embedded AI, shadow AI) within risk appetite: identify the risks from identification constraints and put mitigating measures in place.

4.8.heading: AI Inventory
4.8.summary: Regularly review inventory design so attributes cover newer AI technologies (e.g. agent attributes, guardrails) and third-party AI information.

4.13.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.13.summary: Designate a control function to own the materiality framework and arbitrate or approve ratings, with independent oversight, clear documentation and regular review of assessments.

5.11.heading: Third-Party AI Management
5.11.summary: FI retains accountability for third-party AI; assess transparency, supply chain, concentration, change notification, contingency, legal terms, capabilities and complexity; if residual risk exceeds appetite, limit, suspend or replace the provider.

5.20.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.20.summary: Non-high-materiality use cases may use other documented reviews, such as peer review by qualified individuals not involved in development or deployment.

verdicts.hypothesis: H4(a) no single framework fully covers more than 60% of expectations
verdicts.detail: highest single-framework full coverage is nist_ai_rmf at 49.0%

verdicts.hypothesis: H4(b) the international union leaves at least 10% with no full mapping
verdicts.detail: 18/51 = 35.3% of expectations have no full mapping in ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF or the EU AI Act

verdicts.hypothesis: H4(c) the residue is concentrated in the predicted clauses
verdicts.detail: 4 of 10 residual clauses were predicted: §3.6, §4.4, §4.13, §4.8. Not predicted: §2.2, §2.5, §3.4, §4.1, §5.11, §5.20

threats_to_validity: Mapping is interpretive and performed by one annotator. Every row carries a justification, a confidence flag and a gap note so it can be disputed individually rather than only in aggregate.

The comparison is asymmetric by nature: ISO 42001 certifies a management system, the EU AI Act regulates products through conformity assessment, and the NIST AI RMF is voluntary. 'Full' coverage means an equivalent obligation exists, not that holding one discharges the other.
EU AI Act obligations attach to a system's risk classification, so a mapping may be full for an Annex III high-risk use and irrelevant for everything else.
18 rows are flagged low confidence and are the first place a reader should look to disagree.

The MAS Information Paper predates the Guidelines and reports observed practice rather than imposing expectations, so its high 'full' count says the Guidelines codified existing practice, not that an institution can rely on it.

rq5.question: How many controls, evidence items and estimated person-hours does each materiality tier require, and where is the long tail?
rq5.method: Applicable controls and their evidence items are counted per use case from the control catalogue, then multiplied by a per-item effort estimate that varies with the control's automatability class and a tier multiplier. Institution-level controls are counted once.

estimates.note: These are assumptions, not measurements. They are published so that a reader can substitute their own and recompute. Measuring them would need a user study; see docs/FUTURE_WORK.md.

verdicts.hypothesis: H5(a) Critical requires more than twice the evidence of the lowest tier present (Medium)
verdicts.detail: Critical mean 91.4 evidence items vs Medium mean 92.0; ratio 0.993. The portfolio contains no Low-tier use case, so Medium is substituted for Low and the hypothesis is weaker than written.

verdicts.hypothesis: H5(b) more than half of total effort sits in the semi and doc classes
H5(c) documentation and review is the largest effort category
verdicts.detail: largest category is documentation_and_review at 26.5%; evaluation_and_testing is 16.8%

threats_to_validity: Person-hours are not measured. They are a transparent assumption set, reported in full, and every derived number moves with them.
The portfolio is synthetic and deliberately spans the tier range, so its mix is not representative of any real institution's AI estate.

The portfolio contains no Low-tier use case, because under the default rubric a Generative AI use case cannot be rated Low: GenAI sets Complexity to High and the impact gate permits one level above Impact. H5(a) is therefore tested against Medium rather than Low and is weaker than written.
Effort is counted per evidence item, which treats a one-line attestation and a full validation report as comparable units within a class.
Reuse across use cases is ignored: a data lineage document covering one dataset serves every use case that uses it, so the portfolio total overstates marginal cost.
